items.prompt:
In a group discussion, you should speak _____.
A) all at the same time
B) one at a time

steps: Only one person should speak at a time so everyone can be heard.

items.prompt:
If you do not understand what a classmate said, you should:
A) Ignore it
B) Ask a question to clear it up
items.answer: B) Ask a question to clear it up

steps: Standard 1.SL.A.1c: Ask questions to clear up any confusion about the topics under discussion.

items.prompt:
Leo says, 'I like the book.' Ana says, 'Me too! The rabbit was my favorite part.' Is Ana building on Leo's comment?
A) Yes
B) No

steps: Ana agrees and adds a specific detail about the book — she builds on Leo's comment.

items.prompt:
Which response best 'builds on' a classmate's comment?
Classmate: 'The fox in the story was sneaky.'
A) 'I like foxes.'
B) 'I agree — especially when he tricked the crow into dropping the cheese.'
items.answer: B) 'I agree — especially when he tricked the crow into dropping the cheese.'

steps: Option B agrees and adds a specific example from the text.
Option A changes the topic (likes foxes in general, not the story's fox).

items.prompt:
Read the exchange:
Kai: 'I think the story's lesson is to be honest.'
Mia: 'I see it differently. I think the lesson is to be brave.'
Is this a good conversation?
A) No — disagreeing is not allowed.
B) Yes — respectfully sharing a different opinion with reasoning is a good conversation skill.

steps: Respectfully sharing a different opinion is a positive conversation behavior. Conversations can include different viewpoints.

items.prompt:
During a book discussion, a student only says 'I agree' every time and never adds a new idea. Is she fully meeting the standard for collaborative conversation?
A) Yes — agreeing is participation.
B) No — she needs to add new ideas to build the conversation.

steps: Standard 1.SL.A.1b requires building on others' talk. Only saying 'I agree' without adding anything new does not build the conversation.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion:
Student A: 'I think the main character was brave.'
Student B: 'I agree! She helped her friend even when she was scared.'
Student A: 'What do you mean she was scared?'
Student B: 'In the dark room scene — she was shaking but still kept going.'

Identify which conversation skills are shown in this exchange.
items.answer: Skills shown: (1) Student B builds on Student A's idea with evidence. (2) Student A asks a clarification question. (3) Student B answers the question with a specific detail from the text. (4) Multiple exchanges occur.

steps: Building on idea: Student B agrees and adds evidence (she was scared but helped).
Clarification question: Student A asks 'What do you mean she was scared?' — 1.SL.A.1c.
Answering with detail: Student B provides a specific scene — develops the conversation further.
Multiple exchanges: the conversation goes back and forth more than once — 1.SL.A.1b.

items.prompt: A group discussion goes quiet after each student shares their idea because no one responds to each other. What is the problem, and what is one concrete strategy to fix it?
items.answer: Problem: Students are sharing in parallel (not responding to each other) — the conversation is a series of statements, not a true discussion. Fix: Require each student to connect to or respond to the previous speaker before sharing their own idea (e.g., 'I agree/disagree with [name] because...').

steps: Parallel sharing is not collaborative conversation — it is a series of monologues.
True collaboration requires responses that build on what was just said.
Fix: a sentence-starter rule forces students to connect to the previous speaker.
